title: Comair 3272
summary: Flight 3272 on approach to Detroit descended to 4,000 feet and was instructed to turn left to intercept the localizer. During the turn, the captain noted the low speed indicator and requested more power from the first officer. The aircraft abruptly stalled with a thin rough accretion of ice on the lifting surfaces. The aircraft rolled violently 145 degrees left, right, and left again as the crew lost control. The stall was attributed to inadequate icing procedures and failure to activate de-icing boots.
probable_cause: Aerodynamic stall and loss of control caused by aircraft encountering a thin rough accretion of ice on the wings while operating at a low airspeed in icing conditions. Contributing factors included inadequate FAA standards for icing operations, inadequate Comair procedures for icing conditions, crew failure to activate de-icing boots contrary to manufacturer recommendations, and operation near the lower end of the flight envelope while flaps were retracted.

title: 1997 Israeli helicopter disaster
summary: Two Israeli Air Force Sikorsky S-65C-3 transport helicopters departed Rosh Pina Airport for a mission to southern Lebanon security zone. After collecting troops, both helicopters were cleared to take off at 6:48 PM and hovered awaiting border clearance, which was granted at 6:56 PM. Three minutes later both helicopters disappeared from radar over moshav She'ar Yashuv in northern Israel. The Israeli investigation concluded the rotor of helicopter 357 struck the tail of helicopter 903. Helicopter 357 crashed immediately while the crew of 903 attempted recovery but failed and it crashed as well. All 73 military personnel aboard (two helicopters with crews totaling 8 and 65 passengers) were killed.
probable_cause: Rotor of helicopter 357 struck the tail of helicopter 903 resulting in collision and crash.

title: China Southern Airlines 3456
summary: China Southern Airlines Flight 3456 crashed at Shenzhen Bao'an on May 8, 1997 during a second attempt to land in a severe thunderstorm. The aircraft bounced hard on the first landing attempt and damaged its nose gear, hydraulic systems, and flaps. Debris from the damaged aircraft scattered across the runway. After a go-around with multiple system failures, the crew attempted a second landing on the damaged aircraft with debris contaminating the runway. During the second landing the aircraft skidded off the runway, broke into three pieces and caught fire.

Debris from the first landing contaminated the runway, and the second landing attempt on the damaged aircraft resulted in skidding off the runway.

title: FedEx Express 14
summary: FedEx Flight 14, an MD-11 cargo flight, crashed during landing at Newark after a destabilized flare and captain overcontrol. The aircraft touched down, bounced, and on the second touchdown about 1,100 feet later, the right landing gear snapped and the right engine contacted the runway. Continued right roll broke the right wing spars and inverted the aircraft on fire. The captain made excessive and late pitch control inputs trying to keep the aircraft on the runway. All five crew and jump seat occupants escaped through the cockpit window. The investigation found the probable cause was the captain's overcontrol during landing and failure to go around after a destabilized flare.
probable_cause: The captain's over-control of the aircraft during the landing and his failure to go around after a destabilized flare. Control inputs were too late and too large to stabilize the landing, resulting in excessive sink rate and rightward roll that compressed the right landing gear strut at the second touchdown.

title: Helikopter Service 451
summary: A Eurocopter AS332 Super Puma helicopter crashed into the Norwegian Sea while descending to land on an offshore platform. An engine overspeed light appeared during descent. Subsequent investigation found multiple fatigue cracks in the splined sleeve of the high-speed bendix shaft, which disintegrated and severed the shaft, causing catastrophic overspeed of the right-hand power turbine and burst, destroying both engines. The helicopter became uncontrollable and descended uncontrollably into the sea.
probable_cause: Multiple fatigue cracks in the splined sleeve between the high-speed bendix shaft and right-hand engine, causing shaft disintegration, engine overspeed, turbine burst, and loss of control. Contributing factors were inadequate inspection program and lack of HUMS monitoring; crew could not recognize severity of intermittent overspeed alarm.

title: 1997 Namibia mid-air collision

summary: A German Air Force Tupolev Tu-154M and a USAF Lockheed C-141B Starlifter collided at 35,000 feet over the Atlantic off Namibia. The German aircraft was cruising at the wrong altitude relative to its southbound heading, violating the semicircular altitude rule. Neither aircraft was equipped with TCAS, and the German aircraft was not in contact with Namibian air traffic control due to communication failures. All 33 people aboard both aircraft were killed.

title: Garuda Indonesia 152
summary: Airbus A300 crashed into mountainous woodlands during approach to Medan after the crew became confused about the correct approach direction. Air traffic control issued conflicting instructions and called the aircraft by the wrong callsign, causing the crew to disregard a critical instruction about approach direction. The crew, unfamiliar with the analog flight instrumentation on the A300B4 FFCC, lost vertical awareness while concentrating on lateral changes and descended below the assigned 2000 foot altitude, striking treetops at 1550 feet.
probable_cause: Confusion regarding approach direction resulted in the crew initiating a left turn instead of a right turn during radar vectoring. This confusion, combined with the crew's focus on lateral changes and inadequate vertical monitoring, caused descent below assigned altitude. Contributing factors included poor ATC vectoring, inadequate conversion training for pilots switching between A300 models with different instrumentation, and failure of the GPWS system.

title: Austral Líneas Aéreas 2553
summary: Austral Líneas Aéreas Flight 2553 crashed on the lands of Estancia Magallanes when ice formed inside the pitot tube during descent through a cumulonimbus cloud. The blockage caused an erroneous low airspeed indication, which the crew misinterpreted as engine power loss. The first officer deployed slats to maintain altitude despite the captain's order to reduce speed, causing asymmetric airflow that tore one slat from the aircraft. The aircraft became uncontrollable and crashed at a 70-degree nose-down attitude.

title: SilkAir 185
summary: SilkAir Flight 185 departed Jakarta at 15:37 local time for an 80-minute flight to Singapore. At 16:05, the cockpit voice recorder ceased recording after Captain Tsu stated he was leaving the cockpit to fetch water. The flight data recorder also stopped recording at 16:11. Flight 185 remained level at FL350 until it started a rapid and nearly vertical dive around 16:12. Parts of the aircraft separated from the fuselage due to high forces from the nearly supersonic dive, and the aircraft hit the Musi River, killing all 104 people on board.
probable_cause: The NTSC concluded that the evidence was insufficient to determine a cause. The NTSB concluded that the crash was the result of deliberate flight-control inputs, most likely by the captain. Investigators found that flight inputs had moved the horizontal stabilizer from level flight to a full nose-down descent.

factors.evidence: Investigators found that flight inputs from one of the pilots had moved the stabilizer from level flight to a full nose-down descent.
It is likely that Captain Tsu pulled out the CVR circuit breaker while exiting the cockpit.
The FDR stopped recording at 16:11, and if Captain Tsu was responsible for the crash, he must have devised some excuse to persuade the first officer to leave the flight deck.
The aircraft started a rapid and nearly vertical dive, and parts of the aircraft separated from the fuselage due to high forces from the nearly supersonic dive.

events.text: The Boeing 737 departed Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport's runway 25R for an 80-minute flight to Singapore's Changi Airport.
The cockpit voice recorder ceased recording after Captain Tsu stated he was leaving the cockpit to fetch water.
The flight data recorder stopped recording.
The aircraft started a rapid and nearly vertical dive around 16:12.
The aircraft hit the Musi River near Palembang, Sumatra, and was travelling faster than the speed of sound.

title: United Airlines 826 (1997)
summary: United Airlines Flight 826 encountered severe clear-air turbulence at cruise altitude of 31,000 feet while the fasten seatbelt sign was off. The aircraft dropped approximately 100 feet and rolled to 18 degrees, producing extreme accelerations including a negative G of -0.824g. Crew failed to announce or sound the fasten seatbelt sign when reactivated, leaving passengers unrestrained. One passenger died and 102 were injured by the violent maneuvers.
probable_cause: Clear-air turbulence encounter with inadequate fasten seatbelt sign notification resulted in passenger injuries and fatality.

factors.evidence: severe clear-air turbulence in the area causing sudden drops and rolls
Nobody could remember hearing the typical fasten seat belt chime when the fasten seat belt light came on and no announcements were made in either English or Japanese
fasten seat belt sign was turned on about two minutes before the turbulence event without any announcement
aircraft suddenly dropped around 100 ft, then pitched up and dropped again with extreme negative G of -0.824g causing injuries

events.text: Flight departed Tokyo Narita at 20:30 local time, reached 31,000 ft cruising altitude
Aircraft reported severe clear-air turbulence in area, captain turned on fasten seatbelt sign
Turbulence subsided, fasten seatbelt sign switched off with announcement that turbulence was still possible
Fasten seatbelt sign came on again without any announcement about two minutes before turbulence event
Severe clear-air turbulence event: aircraft dropped, pitched up, rolled 18 degrees right, fell again with peak acceleration 1.814g and minimum -0.824g
Japanese woman found unconscious in aisle with heavy bleeding, died despite resuscitation efforts; fifteen passengers and three flight attendants sustained spine and neck fractures

notes: aircraft subsequently retired; this was last revenue flight
resulted in United Airlines safety bulletin on turbulence procedures
